newsitem.title: USA: State Department official cleared in probe.
newsitem.headline: State Department official cleared in probe.

text.p: A senior State Department official has been cleared of allegations that she engaged in unauthorised disclosure of classified information to foreigners and improperly obtained a security clearance, the department said on Tuesday.

Toby Gati, assistant secretary of state for intelligence and research, was investigated by the department's Inspector General who "has found that both of these charges are without merit," spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
"We consider the matter to be closed," said Burns.
He said Gati remained on the job during the probe and, throughout, has had the "full faith and support" of Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who retired from office as of Monday.

Burns said the investigation also "found no credible information in the course of its investigation indicating impropriety on the part of Charles Gati," the husband of Toby Gati and himself a former employee of the department's policy planning staff.

The charges against the Gatis first appeared last November in the Washington Times newspaper which said Toby Gati was being investigated for "questionable foreign contacts and improperly seeking top-secret documents that link her husband and a family friend to Hungary's spy service."

Among the matters said to be under investigation are claims that Toby Gati, a political appointee and friend of First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton, improperly provided information to Russia's foreign minister and received intelligence data without proper clearances and before being confirmed by the Senate.
The newspaper said at the time that the FBI reviewed the case for criminal wrongdoing or foreign counterespionage activities and decided against launching an investigation.

In announcing the inspector general's findings, Burns said "I feel compelled to come forward and make this announcement because both Toby and Charles Gati found themselves the subject of press speculation and some very high-profile stories in the papers."
But he refused to make the official report available, saying it was not the department's practice to do so.
